name: Clintonism
summary: Clintonism is the New Democrat or Third Way governing approach of Bill Clinton and the Democratic Leadership Council: expand opportunity, not government, pair rights with responsibility, reward work over welfare, expand trade and shrink the deficit, prevent crime and punish criminals, and engage the world.
scope: Bill Clinton's own stated programme as candidate and president (1992 campaign, 1993-2001 speeches and signings) and the DLC New Orleans Declaration (1990) he cites, with the Miller Center scholarship on the record. It excludes the wider global Third Way and later Democratic politics.

furtherReading.note: Clinton explains the New Orleans Declaration.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Clinton's 1993 Health Security plan sought comprehensive, universal coverage guaranteed to every American, though through insurance mandates rather than a single government payer.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: His 1993 plan raised the top federal income tax rate from 31 to 36 percent and added a surtax on the wealthiest, framed as asking them to pay a fair share without 'soaking' the rich.

work-for-welfare.rationale: His central welfare pledge was to end welfare as we know it, making it a second chance not a way of life, with work requirements built into the 1996 law he signed.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: He signed the 1996 law but said its cuts for legal immigrants were far too deep and unrelated to welfare reform's purpose, so he did not hold that benefits should be reserved for citizens.

death-penalty.rationale: He signed the 1994 crime bill extending the federal death penalty to killers of law enforcement officers and the 1996 antiterrorism act on capital appeals.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: He championed 'three strikes and you're out', requiring life sentences for a third violent crime, and signed it in the 1994 crime law.

limit-guns.rationale: He signed the Brady law and campaigned for the assault weapons ban and background checks at gun shows, while framing the aim as keeping guns from criminals.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: The administration's statement on the Defense of Marriage Act says the President has long opposed same-sex marriage and would sign the bill.

abortion-legal.rationale: In accepting the 1992 nomination he said he was pro-choice, strongly, and that the decision belongs to women; he vetoed the 1996 partial-birth ban as drafted.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: His 1993 policy let homosexuals serve but not declare their orientation, which he called a sensible balance between individual rights and military needs; he did not endorse open service.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: His 1995 affirmative-action speech defends active efforts against the continuing effects of discrimination as a means to equal opportunity, with reforms.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: He answered calls to abolish affirmative action with 'mend it, don't end it': he rejected quotas and preferences for the unqualified but kept the programmes.

free-trade.rationale: The New Orleans Declaration calls for expanding trade, not restricting it, and he argued for NAFTA, GATT and China trade as lifting living standards, with labor and environmental conditions attached.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The New Orleans Declaration says the way to economic security is to expand trade, not restrict it, and he pressed China to cut tariffs and subsidies protecting inefficient industries.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: NAFTA was concluded with side agreements on labor standards and the environment that he presented as making it a unique trade agreement.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: His 1993 plan and the 1997 Balanced Budget Act put deficit reduction first, and the New Orleans Declaration stresses growth through fiscal discipline.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: He called a balanced budget amendment unnecessary and unwise because it could cripple the country in an economic crisis.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: He expanded the earned income tax credit as a core means of rewarding work and lifting working families out of poverty.

regulate-corporations.rationale: He backed deregulation (telecommunications) and cutting costly rules yet insisted on national protections for food, toys, nursing homes and cars, so the record points both ways.

corporate-influence.rationale: His campaign-finance proposals aimed at special-interest money: bans on lobbyist contributions, curbs on PACs and an end to soft money.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: He used force or led NATO force in Bosnia, Haiti and Kosovo on humanitarian grounds and the DLC credo commits to forceful stands against ethnic cleansing.

non-intervention.rationale: His interventions in Bosnia, Haiti and Kosovo, defended as protecting people from atrocities, contradict a ban on intervening in another state's internal affairs.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: He ordered strikes on Serbia and sent troops to Haiti, wars of intervention not defence of US territory.

force-without-un.rationale: He said the United States must be prepared to act alone when necessary, and NATO's 1999 campaign against Serbia proceeded on allied authority.

nation-first.rationale: He urged coalitions and international institutions and warned against those who believe America should only act alone, though he kept the option to act alone.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: He enlarged NATO and described the alliance as protecting US security, the opposite of ending permanent alliances.

democratic-peace.rationale: He stated that democracies don't attack each other and made supporting the advance of democracy a pillar of security.

limit-growth.rationale: The New Orleans Declaration holds that economic growth is a prerequisite for opportunity, and he called the choice between the economy and the environment a false choice.

arms-reduction.rationale: He signed the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, cut arsenals under START and extended the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

state-harmful.rationale: He said the era of big government is over but that citizens cannot return to fending for themselves, and government has important responsibilities.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He rejected a minimal state: government must expand opportunity through education, tax credits, health and policing.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: He signed the 1994 crime bill funding 100,000 police and new prisons.

taxation-theft.rationale: He raised income taxes in 1993 as the fair way to share the burden of deficit reduction.

central-planning.rationale: His programme rests on an open market economy: he argued for letting the free market work and for trade expansion.

one-party-rule.rationale: He criticised China as a one-party state restricting free speech and religious expression.

suppress-opposition.rationale: He criticised China for restricting free speech and religious expression.

party-controls-media.rationale: He criticised China for restricting free speech and wanted the internet to open it.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Clinton said Washington's ideological trench warfare produced false choices and set out his approach as a Third Way rooted in common sense and results.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: He described the Third Way as rejecting the old left and right choices (business or labor, economy or environment) in favour of combining their best ideas.

social-market-economy.rationale: The New Orleans Declaration pairs growth and trade with social protection for those left behind: tax credits for work, health care, with national rules to safeguard consumers.

rehabilitation.rationale: The New Orleans Declaration commits to preventing crime and punishing criminals, not explaining away their behavior, and the 1994 law toughened sentences.

religious-exemptions.rationale: He signed the Religious Freedom Restoration Act in 1993, which protects religious practice from being burdened by general government action.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The New Orleans Declaration commits to the politics of inclusion and the protection of civil rights for all Americans.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Clinton repeatedly asked Congress to raise the minimum wage but described what he backed as a modest increase (SOTU 1995: weight of the evidence is that a modest increase does not cost jobs; 1999: a dollar over two years), not a substantial one.
